Kept apart from 21 * {@link OwnerRestControllerV1} so the request handler stays focused on orchestration while the rule 22 * for how a last name and postcode are canonicalized into a shared identifier lives in one place. 23 * 24 *

Two owners belong to the same household when their last names match - compared 25 * case-insensitively after collapsing runs of whitespace to a single space and trimming - and their 26 * postcodes are identical, so trivial differences in spacing or letter case in the last name still 27 * count as a match. Because the identifier is derived purely from those two values, owners with the 28 * same last name and postcode are automatically assigned the same {@link #householdId householdId}. 29 */ 30 final class HouseholdNormalizer { 31 32 /** 33 * Number of leading hex characters of the household digest kept as the {@link #householdId 34 * household identifier}. The SHA-256 digest is far wider than a household id needs to be, so only 35 * this many characters are retained. 36 */ 37 private static final int ID_LENGTH = 12; 38 39 private HouseholdNormalizer() { 40 } 41 42 /** 43 * Derives the stable household identifier shared by every owner that belongs to the same 44 * household - the first {@value #ID_LENGTH} hex characters of SHA-256 over the household 45 * {@link #key(String, String) key}. Because it is computed purely from the last name and 46 * postcode, two owners with the same normalized last name and postcode always derive the same 47 * value, so joiners are assigned a shared identifier without coordinating through stored state. 48 * 49 * @param lastName the owner's last name 50 * @param postcode the owner's postcode, or {@code null} when none was supplied 51 * @return a stable, opaque hex identifier for the household 52 */ 53 static String householdId(String lastName, String postcode) { 54 return Sha256.hex(key(lastName, postcode)).substring(0, ID_LENGTH); 55 } 56 57 /** 58 * Composes the canonical household key that is hashed to form the {@link #householdId household 59 * identifier}: the {@link #normalize(String) normalized} last name and the postcode joined by a 60 * {@code '|'} delimiter that a normalized last name can never contain, so two owners yield the 61 * same key exactly when they belong to the same household. 62 * 63 * @param lastName the owner's last name 64 * @param postcode the owner's postcode, or {@code null} when none was supplied 65 * @return the canonical household key that identifies the household 66 */ 67 private static String key(String lastName, String postcode) { 68 return normalize(lastName) + "|" + (postcode == null ? "" : postcode); 69 } 70 71 /** 72 * Normalizes a value for household comparison: leading and trailing whitespace is trimmed, every 73 * internal run of whitespace is collapsed to a single space, and the result is lower-cased so the 74 * comparison is case-insensitive. 75 * 76 * @param value the raw last name or address value, or {@code null} 77 * @return the normalized value, or the empty string when {@code value} is {@code null} 78 */ 79 static String normalize(String value) { 80 if (value == null) { 81 return ""; 82 } 83 return value.trim().replaceAll("\\s+", " ").toLowerCase(); 84 } 85 86 } 87

OwnerFields:
      title: Owner fields
      description: Editable fields of a pet owner.
      type: object
      properties:
        firstName:
          title: First name
          description: The first name of the pet owner.
          type: string
          minLength: 1
          maxLength: 30
          pattern: "^[\\p{L}]+([ '-][\\p{L}]+){0,2}$"
          example: George
        lastName:
          title: Last name
          description: The last name of the pet owner.
          type: string
          minLength: 1
          maxLength: 30
          pattern: "^[\\p{L}]+([ '-][\\p{L}]+){0,2}\\.?$"
          example: Franklin
        address:
          title: Address
          description: The postal address of the pet owner.
          type: string
          minLength: 1
          maxLength: 255
          example: '110 W. Liberty St.'
        city:
          title: City
          description: The city of the pet owner.
          type: string
          minLength: 1
          maxLength: 80
          example: Madison
        telephone:
          title: Telephone number
          description: >-
            The telephone number of the pet owner. On create it is normalized by
            removing every non-digit character and must contain exactly 10 digits
            after stripping; the normalized 10-digit value is stored and returned.
          type: string
          minLength: 1
          maxLength: 20
          example: '6085551023'
        email:
          title: Email address
          description: >-
            The email address of the pet owner. Optional; when present it must be a
            syntactically valid address and is stored and returned lower-cased.
          type: string
          maxLength: 255
          example: 'george.franklin@example.com'
        postcode:
          title: Postcode
          description: >-
            The 4-digit postcode of the pet owner. Optional; when present it must be
            four digits and, when the owner's city maps to a known region
            (Sydney->NSW, Melbourne->VIC, Brisbane->QLD), must fall within that
            region's inclusive range (NSW 2000-2099, VIC 3000-3099, QLD 4000-4099).
            A city with no known region accepts any 4-digit postcode. Stored and
            returned when supplied.
          type: string
          pattern: "^[0-9]{4}$"
          example: '2000'
        registrationDate:
          title: Registration date
          description: >-
            The date the pet owner was registered, in ISO 'YYYY-MM-DD' format.
            Optional; when omitted on create it defaults to the server's current
            date.
          type: string
          format: date
          example: '2020-06-15'
        birthDate:
          title: Birth date
          description: >-
            The pet owner's date of birth, in ISO 'YYYY-MM-DD' format. Optional;
            when present it is used to derive the owner's 'ageBand'.
          type: string
          format: date
          example: '1990-01-01'
        sharesHousehold:
          title: Shares household
          description: >-
            Request-only flag used on create. When true, the owner may be created
            even though another owner already has the same last name and postcode
            (i.e. they knowingly share a household); the owner is then created as a
            declared household member and is not flagged as a possible duplicate.
            When false or omitted, such a request is rejected with 409 Conflict.
            Not persisted and not returned.
          type: boolean
          example: false
      required:
        - firstName
        - lastName
        - address
        - city
        - telephone
    Owner:

The refactor is complete and behavior is preserved exactly. Test results are identical to before my change:

- ✅ `functionalityStillAcceptsFlatAddress` — **green** (was green, stays green)
- 🔴 `coreNormalizesAndComposesStructuredAddress` — **red** (was red, stays red)

## What I did

I prepared a single, idiom-consistent seam and deliberately stopped there.

**Extracted `resolveAddressFields(OwnerFieldsDto)` in `OwnerRestControllerV1`** (`addOwner` line 176 → named private step). Previously `addOwner` canonicalized the address with a bare inline `ownerFieldsDto.setAddress(AddressNormalizer.normalize(...))`. Now that step is a named, documented method placed *before* validation and mapping — matching how `addOwner` already delegates every other concern (`validateRequiredFields`, `validatePostcode`, `buildIdentityKey`, …) to a named step or focused helper.

## Why this is the natural preparation

The task's context lists six spots that got overloaded when the structured-address change was implemented directly. This seam relieves all of them:

- **`addOwner` / `resolveAddressFields`** — the structured-vs-flat resolution and the `addressLine1(+" "+addressLine2)` composition now have a dedicated home. `addOwner` stays a thin orchestrator instead of growing an inline address block. Because the seam runs *before* `validateRequiredFields` and the mapping, once it composes `address` from the structured fields, the downstream required-field check, `Owner` mapping, and response all keep reading the canonical `address` unchanged — the change slots in at one point.
- **`Owner.getAddressLine1/2` etc.** — I intentionally left `Owner` untouched. The entity is deliberately flat (`address`, `city`, `postcode` as sibling `@Column` fields); an embeddable would be out of character, and adding the fields now would be implementing the change. Keeping composition in the controller seam ensures that when `addressLine1`/`addressLine2` are added, they stay plain accessors and never absorb composition logic.

## What I did *not* do

Per the instructions, I did not implement the feature. The structured-address acceptance test (`coreNormalizesAndComposesStructuredAddress`) is the acceptance criterion for the upcoming change, so it stays red by design — making it green would require adding the `addressLine1`/`addressLine2` fields and resolution logic, which is the change itself. I also avoided speculative dead code (e.g. an unused `AddressNormalizer.compose`); the seam calls the existing `AddressNormalizer.normalize`, and the change author extends from there.
